newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: FEATURE - Sri Lanka takes fresh path to marsh conservation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sri Lanka takes fresh path to marsh conservation.

text.p: The wild water fowl begin to caw in the pre-dawn gloom, a few hours before the marsh's other inhabitants awaken.
Then as a ray of morning sunshine filters through the canopy of mist and shimmers on the water, Muthurajawela, Sri Lanka's largest single expanse of marsh, slowly stirs to life.

Water lilies part to make way for our boat and the little white flowers of the anona plant fall into our laps as we glide past thick marsh vegetation towards one of this Indian Ocean island's most impressive mangrove forests.
The verdant calm seems a world away from the carnage of Sri Lanka's civil war, which caused tourist arrivals to the island to plunge 30 percent in the first nine months of the year.
Sri Lankan officials hope Muthurajawela -- touted as a rare balance between ecological and economic needs -- will help bring those tourists back.
"This is no conventional safari. Sorry, there are no elephants and leopards here," said the Department of Wildlife Conservation's Vasabha Vattala, the manager of the marsh's visitor centre.
"But what we do offer is a very fulfilling experience with nature," Vattala told Reuters.

Muthurajawela's 6,232 hectares (15,000 acres) are a nursery for coastal fish and home to some 126 species of birds -- 40 of them migratory fowl -- and is the 'green lung' for the congested capital, Colombo, on whose northern outskirts the wetland borders.
But the marsh is also home to more than 4,000 families, many of them from a long line of marsh-dwellers.

"Conservation cannot stand by itself. It has to be linked to development that supports economic growth," said Dr. Jayampathy Samarakoon of the Central Environmental Authority, a consultant for the Muthurajawela Wetland Conservation Project.
"At least in Asia, this is one of the few conservation projects that distinctly tries to harmonise environmental management with economic development," he said.
Born as a tropical wetland some 5,000 years ago, the marshy expanse was used later as a huge rice-growing field by kings as early as the 15th century.
But that ended after efforts to build a canal linking Colombo with another port town inadvertently loosed a flood of sea water into the wetlands during the l7th and 18th centuries.

As our boat meanders through the waterways we come face to face with the local human inhabitants, the reasons management of the marsh became necessary. Children play in knee-deep, brackish water while their parents, mostly fishermen, dry salted fish in the sun outside their mud huts.

"If they had the means, they would not be living in the marsh. So instead of evicting them, we have thought of providing them with alternative means in order to cut down on their dependence on the marsh," Samarakoon said.

Four percent of the marsh's area has been reclaimed for development. About 280 families have been given permanent housing on that land at a cost to the government of about 22 million rupees ($385,000).
Part of the reclaimed area has also been opened to business investment and has already attracted considerable interest given its proximity to Colombo.
The marsh is separated from the developed land by a buffer zone equal to six percent of Muthurajawela's total land area.
The government-initiated effort has consolidated 17 dispersed communities into a handful of larger ones, reducing pollution and providing marsh-dwellers with access to sewage and drainage systems.
"The whole exercise has cost us about 60 million rupees ($1.05 million), which is minor by today's conservation standards," said Samarakoon.
The project also instructs the marsh-dwellers on ways to protect the marsh's fragile ecosystem.
"We tell them why they should not catch small fish, why they should be allowed to live to grow and multiply," Vattala said.
Villagers are encouraged to reduce their fish catch and to grow crops in plots of land in the buffer zone, he added.
"The ecological restoration is just starting. As dwellers begin to move into housing from surviving on the land, the ecology should improve," Samarakoon said. ($=57 rupees)
